messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan was nineteen, single, and working the evening shift at a fast-food restaurant when the storm hit his coastal town and turned the streets into a roaring gray river. He had been closing up with two coworkers when the wind started driving rain sideways through the parking lot, the lights flickered, and the windows rattled hard enough that everyone stopped talking. By the time he got home, the neighborhood had already lost power. Water crept through the front door, carrying mud, broken branches, and the sour smell of gasoline and wet drywall. In the dark, he could hear sirens, neighbors shouting, and the grinding crash of a tree coming down somewhere nearby. Afterward, what stayed with him were not full scenes but flashes: the doorway buckling under the pressure of water, the kitchen floating with ruined food and chairs, the image of his mother standing barefoot in the hall with a flashlight, and, when he thought about it, the same damp smell rising back up as if he were there again. Remembering it brought the terror back with the same force he had felt that night, a sudden tightening in his chest and the certainty that the next disaster could come without warning.

In the weeks that followed, Ethan began to think of himself as permanently changed. He had been a happy person before, he would say, someone who joked with coworkers and could handle a busy rush, but now he felt unrecognisable to himself, “miserable” in a way that seemed to have settled into him for good. The more he replayed the storm in fragments, the more he concluded that something in him had broken that could not be repaired. Those memories were mostly pictures in his mind, brief and vivid: water against the door, the smashed fence, a sheet of rain in the streetlight. Sometimes the images came with the smell of wet wood and mud so sharply that he would stop what he was doing and look around, unsettled by how real it felt. Because the memories could bring back the terror so quickly, he tried hard not to think about the storm at all. He kept himself busy, pushed the images away when they surfaced, and avoided anything that might feel stressful, telling himself that staying clear of upsetting situations was the only way to keep from falling apart again.

That strategy, though, left Ethan increasingly dependent on managing himself before every interaction. At work he rehearsed conversations in his head before speaking to a manager, a customer, or even a coworker at the fryer, running through what he should say so he would not be caught off guard. He did the same before calling home or answering his phone, worried that if he stumbled he would seem weak or unstable. He had come to believe that the person he had become was not the same person others had known, and that belief made him watch himself closely, checking for signs that he was slipping further into this damaged version of himself. The more he tried to avoid stress and stay composed, the more he noticed his own awkwardness and the more certain he became that the storm had permanently altered him for the worse. A brief delay in the drive-thru, a raised voice from a supervisor, even the sight of dark clouds over the parking lot could set off the same uneasy self-scrutiny. At home, too, he became careful and distant, wanting nothing that might stir up the memories, which only made him feel more cut off from the easier, happier version of himself he remembered.

By the time he came for help, Ethan was tired of living around his own reactions. He had started missing small parts of work and pulling back from friends because he was afraid of being overwhelmed in front of them. What brought him in was the growing fear that he would keep shrinking his life to avoid reminders of the storm and end up losing whatever was left of the person he used to be. He hoped therapy might help him stop feeling permanently ruined, but what frightened him most was the possibility that the terror would keep coming back every time an image, a smell, or a stressful moment broke through his efforts to hold it away.
